utterances.text: Let's have a look at it. It reads: "Zoran Subotic was replaced by Zoran Pazin as commander of the TO who was soon arrested and replaced by Marko Pavlovic." Now, tell us what game you played here and why it is not true because you gave an answer which the OTP wanted to hear and which is not in accordance with the truth? Let's take it one by one; was Zoran Subotic replaced by Zoran Pazin as commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is correct, however, in the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was Zoran Pazin soon arrested and then replaced by Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that statement is fully correct, if I understand you well. If we are talking about your testimony, we'll deal with that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, bullet point 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have drawn our attention to it. In view of the -- in view of the testimonies, we'll discuss that at later stage. We, at this moment, focus on your statement. Any other matter in your statement at this moment where you can point at an answer which is not truthful and explained by you as a result of playing games?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. I don't know, there's nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you reviewed this statement before you came to court and that you spent another half an hour on it during the last break; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P1623 in evidence be brought up to the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, I am going to ask that you be shown a photograph in which one person in the photograph is circled. I would like you to focus on the person who is circled and tell us if you recognise that person. If it assists you in determining whether you recognise this person, I can show you a short video-clip in which this person is walking. The photo on the screen before you is a still photo made from that video. Do you recognise the person who is circled?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: This is not a very good photo, is it? I really don't recognise the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am going to ask that 65 ter 596 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that 65 ter 596.3 be played for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will play the video for which this still photograph is taken and you will see the person enter the room. See if this assists you in whether you recognise the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can see the person enter the room now. Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I'm not sure but I believe that that was Arkan's Major Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the record is clear, when you are identifying someone as Arkan's Major Peja, is that the person who was circled in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see this person in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the first time you saw this person in Zvornik was?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I saw him in Bijeljina even before that. I'm not sure about the date. I believe that it was either on the 5th or 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what circumstances you saw this person in Bijeljina on that approximate date?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, that was a day after an armed conflict broke out in Bijeljina, the JNA barracks came under attack and that developed into a fully-blown conflict. They asked for help. I was sent to Bijeljina where Arkan's Unit was and my task was to bring them over to Zvornik and to billet them there to help us because we requested assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've just testified that you were sent to Bijeljina. Who sent you to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, we called that the department of the ministry for looking after non-Serbs and Mr. Bogdanovic was in charge. I was referred to Mr. Kostic, I called him and he told me to go to Bijeljina to find a man whose name was Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is the first name of the person you've just referred to as Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Radoslav or Rade Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With as much precision as you are able, what did Rade Kostic tell you when he sent you to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago so I can only tell you that that was more or less what he told me. That Arkan's Unit was in Bijeljina, that I should report to them, to tell them that we had a problem in Zvornik, and that they should go from Bijeljina to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time that you were instructed to go to Bijeljina, do you know if the decision had already been made to send Arkan to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I don't know whether such a decision had been made. That was the first time I ever heard of Arkan. Actually, I had bought a newspaper at the news stand, the Sarajevo Oslobodjenje and the front page depicted a photo from Bijeljina. There was a dead body on the street, somebody was kicking that dead body and the title was "War in Bijeljina, Arkan plunders and murders." That was the title on the front page of that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A few minutes ago on page 53 at line 18 you said the following: "My task was to bring them over to Zvornik and to billet them there." At the time you were sent up to Bijeljina, was it your understanding that you were to make arrangements for their billeting in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, you see, let me tell you this: My task was to seek assistance. We couldn't billet them in Zvornik because Zvornik had been occupied by Muslims. All of us Serbs had been expelled by Zvornik; we could not even come close to the city and that's why we billeted them in a hotel across the river from Zvornik and the name of the hotel is Radaljska Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your prior evidence in your statement of 2008, you describe two visits of Biljana Plavsic to Zvornik, the first one before the outbreak of conflict and the second one after. Can I ask you to assist us with the chronology of when you went to Bijeljina, was it before or after Ms. Plavsic's first visit to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: My departure to Bijeljina has nothing to do with Biljana Plavsic's visit to Zvornik. I went to Bijeljina in order to seek assistance from Arkan and his volunteers. I wanted them to come to Zvornik. Biljana Plavsic visited Zvornik for the first time before the fighting broke out. It could have been either the 7th or the 8th of April, 1992. I do know that when I left to Bijeljina to see Arkan, Fikret Abdic had been to Bijeljina and that's what they told us back in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us which members of Arkan's organisation you spoke with in Bijeljina about coming to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I went to the community centre in Bijeljina. There were quite a few people there from Bijeljina whom I know and quite a few of those who I didn't know who wore uniforms. At one point a man entered the room, everybody sprang to their feet. Somebody said it was Arkan. I approached him, introduced myself to him, described to him what the problem was that we had in Zvornik, and then he instructed the men we saw on the photograph, Pejic, to take some 20 men and to follow me to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was Major Peja present at that time?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who did you believe Arkan worked for at that time?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I think that more than anything else he worked for his own benefit. But I also know that he arrived in Zvornik at the time with a licence plate of the federal SUP because normally you could tell by the first number of the licence plate to whom -- who it belonged to. I saw that his licence plate had "9" as the first number which denoted that it was from the federal level. So he came to Zvornik in the official car of the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there any other letters or numbers from that licence plate that you recall?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I think that in one of the statements I even stated the number, but I can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your prior evidence you describe volunteers arriving from Serbia. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did they arrive in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Among other things there were several calls from our Crisis Staff in Zvornik and from various political parties which dispatched their volunteers as well as from some groups that were arriving. For the most part these were volunteers which had had some combat experience at the front line in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did they arrive in Zvornik? Did they take their own transportation, was transportation provided for them? What was the means on which they came?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: There were various means of transportation, some came with their own vehicles, others with organised transport, for others it would be the Crisis Staff that would organise. If there was a group of volunteer appearing at the Crisis Staff, we would arrange transportation for them. There were also instances where political parties would get involved as well if they supported this sort of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did some of these people arrive with their own weapons?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I believe that some did, yes, because they had already been to the front line in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For those in the courtroom who may not be familiar with the geography of Zvornik, is it true that the river Drina flows along the border between Bosnia and Serbia through Zvornik, and the Bosnian portion of Zvornik is on the west bank and Mali Zvornik, which lies in Serbia, is on the east bank? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes. The Drina is a administrative border between Serbia and Bosnia throughout the territory of the Zvornik municipality. We are now discussing a period of time when Bosnia had not yet been recognised. In our mind this was one state, one territory because the JNA was still present in Zvornik in the time-period we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. I think Mr. Groome wanted to know whether the Drina separated the Mali Zvornik from the Bosnian Zvornik and I think you have answered that question by your first yes and by the following sentence. Mr. Groome, please proceed. Could you please focus your answers very much on what is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your prior evidence, you describe the relationship Marko Pavlovic had with the Serbian state security service. Can I ask you to describe that for us today?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I described how I came to meet him. We were at the ministry for the Serbs outside of Serbia. We saw that the war was in the offing and based on some historical experience, we asked for them to procure weapons for us. They told us that we should report to Darda at Kostic's. That was when I met Marko Pavlovic. I know that his name at the time was Branko Popovic. He was the TO commander for the town of Darda. Since at that point the hostilities had come to a stop in the Republic of Croatia, he moved to Zvornik where he assisted us in the arming effort because he had very good connections in the JNA. It's common knowledge that the Tuzla Corps headed by General Sabo Jankovic, its commander, was aware of his stay in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask a few different questions. You've identified this person as having two names, do you know which was his rightful name and if you do, tell us which one it was?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I know his real name is Branko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he begin using the name Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, the first time I heard him use the name was when the conflict in Zvornik broke out, when he was introduced to us as Major Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know why he began to use an alias when he took up duties in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, he used a false name and a false rank probably to protect his identity in order for it not to be revealed. To my knowledge, he was not a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: At some point, perhaps in June of 1992, he and a group of volunteers were arrested in Zvornik. This came as a great surprise to us because he was a person of great authority in that community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who arrested him?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: He was arrested by the police of the Republika Srpska. As far as I know, he spent several days in the prison in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he released after spending several days in the prison in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Zuca?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, he led a group of volunteers in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the name of the group of volunteers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know Zuca's full name?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Vojin Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he also arrested?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes. He was arrested together with the group including Marko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He was arrested at the same time as Marko Pavlovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about the same person, Branko Popovic, Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he also released after two to three days?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: As far as I know they were all released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that we are nearing the break. Could I ask that the witness be escorted out, there is a brief matter I'd like to discuss with the Chamber before I continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break but you'll first be escorted out of the the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in half an hour, Witness JF-026.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recognise that we are in an unusual predicament at the moment. If -- how I continue with my examination would depend upon the Chamber's decision on the 92 ter, I only have a few more questions if the evidence is accepted in 92 ter. So I would appreciate some guidance whether to continue asking some more detailed questions but I feel after not a very long period of time I've -- I would have come to the junction that I would -- it would be important to know, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you asked for guidance, not for a decision yet, and the Chamber at this moment would give you the guidance that you, as we said before, you can proceed as if a 92 ter application was appropriately been made. Now, that hasn't changed since I said that. However, the Chamber reserves its right to finally decide on the matter, but in view of this guidance, if during cross-examination there suddenly other reasons would arise why the Chamber would be unwilling to accept the 92 ter application, then an additional opportunity will be given to you to further examine the witness. So by acting on the basis of the assumption that 92 ter might appropriately be applied, if that assumption turns out finally not to be true, then an additional opportunity will be given to you to elicit further evidence which is then missing because you couldn't apply 92 ter. Is that sufficient guidance?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is, Your Honours, that's helpful. Can I ask that the Chamber consider during the break, I do have a copy of the

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: exhibits he gave evidence about, whether the Chamber would consider directing him to review that tonight and making notes in the margin and then giving me an opportunity to go through any corrections tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I earlier said that we'll deal with the transcript at the a later stage that was one of the things that the Chamber, I with the other judges, had on our mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this raise any questions or further comments? If not, we'll take a break and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The material Mr. Groome wanted to give to the witness has been inspected by the Defence teams as far as I understand, therefore, Madam Registrar is instructed to provide the hard copy to the witness at the end of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, I now want to draw your attention to the portion of your evidence in which you describe the second visit of Mrs. Plavsic after the outbreak of conflict. In response to a question in the first case about what was discussed with her, you had said the following, I'm quoting from the bottom of 21209: "I informed her as far as I knew about the situation in Zvornik after it was placed under the control of the Serbs of Zvornik and she inquired as to the extent to which we were implementing the plans, how organised we were." My question is the following: When you said implementing the plans, what plans were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, it's generally known that the Serbian Democratic Party,

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: already evident, drafted a plan of activity and in view of what Bosnia-Herzegovina was like, there was a plan A which referred to the areas where Serbs were in a majority and where they were already in power, and I am talking about the local authorities, and there was a plan B relating to the areas where the Serbs were a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which version or plan A or plan B did you inform her you were implementing?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: We were in a minority in Zvornik. The Muslim population was in the majority and according to the instructions, we had a plan B to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, what aspects of plan B did you inform her had been successfully implemented?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Given that the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was detrimental for us, we proceeded to implement plan B which meant that all the territories where there were Serbs would be placed under Serb control, the police force would be split into Serb and Muslim forces, and a number of other activities that I can't recall at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Could I ask the Defence who is going to cross-examine the witness first? Mr. Petrovic, it's you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Petrovic, when I early was a -- earlier was a bit critical about that you didn't stop speaking, I appreciate it very much that you continued after that in English, apparently fully understanding what my concern was at the time. That's appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to apologise to you once again because I didn't understand your intervention properly at first but I would like to proceed with my cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't seeking further apologies. I wanted to express my appreciation for what you did immediately after that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that that wasn't what you were seeking, but I felt the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will have some questions for you and I kindly ask you to answer them, but please be mindful of the break that you must make between question and answer because we speak the same language. Tell me, witness, when did you get in touch with the Prosecution of the ICTY for the first time? Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: 1999 or perhaps 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this first contact was like?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: They invited me to come to Budapest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did you go to Budapest? What was it like? Who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: The problem which is present in all these statements is that it was always somebody else and then you always had to correct them and explain it them that Slavonia was not Slovenia, that Slavonia was where it was, because they kept confusing these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On this occasion in 1998 or 1999 did you give a statement, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what sort of status did you have, legally speaking, in 1998, 1999, 2000, how did they treat you, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: As a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you understand the fact that you were regarded as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, I already referred to it in passing. I believe that I was one step to being indictment -- indicted and I wanted to be as forthcoming as possible in my contacts with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, there was this possibility open at all times for you to be indicted, is that how you understood the situation to legally be?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, nobody told me that in so many words, but I did feel this possibility hanging over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you know, up until what time did you hold the status of suspect? I observe that during your testimony in case 2 you were also accompanied by a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: At that time I also gave a statement as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that the fact that for full ten years you were treated as a suspect had a bearing on the weight of your evidence. Can you explain in what way this was?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, we from the local level wanted to appear interesting to the Prosecution and to achieve this we mentioned names of individuals whom we never met in person. We tried to snuggle up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, one second. Your last question was translated as having a bearing on the weight of your evidence. Of course the weight is of evidence, I don't know whether, you used the equivalent in your own language, but of course the weight is only to be decided by a court. But apparently the witness understood your question as being, and it may have been that that was your question, in what way his position as a suspect influenced the answers he gave when interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question may have not been interpreted properly. I never thought for a moment, nor did I say that I considered the legal weight of the evidence. I just asked the witness whether his status had a bearing on the contents and he answered. I will continue with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you shared the things with the Prosecutor that he perhaps wanted to hear. What is it, in your view, that the Prosecutor wanted to hear from you and is now mentioned in this statement?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: These are the things that I mentioned and I did not participate in those things directly. I drew conclusions based on the things that I heard about people whom I had never seen or spoken to. Serbia had a status that it had been the international framework. We were popular and we all competed in smearing Milosevic, smearing the regime and everything it represented. That's what we all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that it was popular to speak about the involvements of Serbia in the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that be one of those facts that you are mentioning now?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You didn't say that you were popular, but rather that it was very popular to present claims about Serbia, Milosevic and his regime?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, you did and it was all done in a very negative context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You thought that if you presented a fact, for example, about the Serbian police, that that might have a bearing on changing your position before the OTP, changing it for the better; right?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the facts that you presented about, for example, the Serbian police, those were not things that you knew firsthand, those were just rumours or unverified information or a combination of what you read in the papers and what you heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: worked as a police employee. I joined another company. I was no longer a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Within that context that we have now before us, when you spoke about the Serbian police, this is not your direct knowledge; right?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: No, this was not my direct knowledge. This was a combination of rumours, newspaper articles, only the things that I participated in myself I describe with a hundred per cent accuracy. As for the rest, I really don't know why we needed all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you told us earlier today that in your statements there are certain things that are correct, however, that the intention or the intonation of the statement itself does not reflect what you wanted to say, is that what you were saying, that you described your participation very accurately, but everything else falls under the category of rumours and speculations?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Precisely so, maybe I could not describe it as accurately as you did now in legal terms. I describe accurately only those things that I participated in. Everything else was my free interpretation which might have led to erroneous conclusions amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions you used the pronoun "we," are you referring to some of your colleagues who participated in the events and who were in a similar or even the identical position?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Precisely so. All of us who were at a local level close to fire, those of us who were close to some incidents and events at a local level, that's who I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are in closed session, sir, could you please give us a name of the people who were involved in those events and who portrayed the events in the same way while they provided the statements and while there was still a threat upon you and your personal safety?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Those were mostly members of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik, Radic, Grujic, Savic, Ivanovic, and some others whom I can't remember at the moment. I can't remember all of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I'm mistaken, but I don't recall where the evidence said that he felt there was a threat to his personal safety. Maybe Mr. Petrovic could indicate where that came in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A misinterpretation. I said legal status, not personal safety.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please turn his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you are invited to turn your microphone on, but that has been done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Petrovic kindly turn on and off his microphone himself because we cannot hear the beginning and end of his sentences because his colleague is doing it for him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got the point that before you start talking about the microphone should be on and it should not be switched off before you have finished. And the tandem work is appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned certain names. Does this refer to a person whose name is Goran Zugic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about Vojislav Jekic, the late Vojislav Jekic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes. All those persons were involved in the events and they had the same problem of relationship with The Hague Tribunal as I did. It was a personal problem for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how was your 2008 statement created, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: It was created here in the offices of the Tribunal. There is a video-clip, there is an audio recording of that statement. We went through my previous statements and then 114 bullet points were drafted, I signed them. I didn't wait for the statement to be printed because I was in a hurry to catch my flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is not a result of an interview, but rather this is a compilation of various prior statements that you provided between 1998 and 2008, did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, they made an excerpt from all the prior statements of all the things that they found interesting and that is a collection of all those numerous prior statements that I had provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, this is a selection but who made that selection, who chose the paragraphs that we see today?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: It was done at the OTP's proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To my learned friend's question you spoke about the plans of the SDS, plan A and plan B, that is first of all, could you please tell us what was your position in the SDS? Were you a high official, a local official? What was your status within the party?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I was a local official in Zvornik municipality. I was the deputy president of the SDS, or rather, the deputy president of the Municipal Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your position did you participate in formulating the SDS policies, did you participate in the work of the SDS for -- at the highest levels?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As a local party member, in addition to what was general knowledge, did you have any information about what was being decided, what was being considered at the top of the party that formulated policies for the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question in this respect. You talked about the instructions, plan A, plan B, was that not decided on the SDS highest levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received that as an instruction, as a written instructions from the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if a question is put to you, did you have any information about what was being decided, what was being considered at the top of the party that formulated parties for the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that plan A and B not be an example of what was decided on the highest levels for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that was a decision made at the very top of the party and applied to the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as a local official, I didn't participate in the passing of that decision. I didn't know who participated in that; we just received that instruction to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did everyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina know about those plans or were they to some extent secret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as soon as the plans were distributed to several hundreds of people, I suppose that they were no longer secret. But on the other hand, I believe that they were internal party documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were not general knowledge, but it was limited to local and central party leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, those documents were distributed along the party lines, among the party members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore the question which Mr. Petrovic put to you whether you had any information about what was decided beyond what was of general knowledge, should have been yes instead of no, if only for this example, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have completely lost me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll put it again to you. Mr. Petrovic asked you:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: that formulated policies for the entire state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?" You said you had no information, but the example shows that you did have information, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, you are not right. I didn't have any information. As for plans A and B, we received those as a written instruction from the party and that instruction was distributed among Municipal Boards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what is found in plan A and B, therefore, was what was decided by the high party level for the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then your answer should have been not a simple no. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you know anything about the reasons behind the passing of the party documents of this kind such as plan A and B?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, the explanation was that this was due to an overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the pre-existing situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDA was a majority, they centralised their power and that was our response to that centralisation of the entire power which was in the hands of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are saying that that document was considered at the municipal SDS board meeting, kindly tell us how many people were involved in the municipal SDS board meeting where that was considered?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: About 50 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether that document was submitted only to your Municipal Board or also to some other Municipal Boards in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I heard that it had been submitted to some other Municipal Boards in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Municipal Boards of the SDS were there approximately in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Almost every municipality had a board which means there were 110 Municipal Boards because this is exactly how many municipalities there were in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are privy to the contents of the plan and you told us how you became familiar with the contents thereof and you said that for your municipality you have just told us that, that Variant B of the plan applied to your municipality. Tell us, please, that Variant B -- I apologise, first of all, could you tell us what you remember from the contents of Variant B, what was to be done, what were you supposed to do in conformity with the B plan submitted to you by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: The documents had some ten bullet points and spoke about the protection and salvation of the Serbian people and all those who supported Yugoslavia who were not in favour of the Yugoslavia breaking up. It was still a whole state. It was still not a rump Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in that plan, do you remember whether there was a reference to the expulsion of non-Serbs or anything even worse that should be done to those people?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: No, plan B did not envisage any measures against any ethnic group or any individual or any group or party. That plan only spoke about the protection of Serbs and the survival of Serbs in the territories that -- where they resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at the time when that plan reached you, just briefly, what was the political situation like in Bosnia-Herzegovina when that plan was created, when it was submitted to you, what was the political situation like?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: That plan was created as a consequence of the division of powers and the centralisation of power on the part of the SDA and that was a situation that existed even before the war, that preceded the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did that plan envisage the establishment of a Crisis Staff in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, that plan envisaged that. We did establish a Crisis Staff, but the SDA also had a Crisis Staff and we shared the same building. Our offices were next to each other. We almost shared the offices, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And your Crisis Staff, therefore, shared the same building as the SDA Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: We were next door to each other and the only thing between the two offices was a plaster-of-paris partition. The building was the so-called Russian building in Zvornik in the -- on the ground floor of that building, the two offices, theirs and ours were on the ground floor of the so-called Russian building in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they know that you were sitting there, did you know that they were sitting in their office?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you knew all those people, did you not? You had known them all your life?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can I then assume that they knew what you were up to and vice-versa, that you knew what they were up to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Precisely so. And we even discussed those things openly amongst each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And your colleagues from the SDA staff probably knew that there was a plan, that you had a plan that would be put in place if Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you also -- you actually told us just now that you discussed things with them very openly, that they were familiar with the details of the things that we are talking about here today?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Just before the war Radovan Karadzic held a rally in Zvornik and the president of the Bosniak organisation, Zulfikar Alipasic [phoen] was there and he said that should Muslims decide to leave Bosnia, that we had a plan as to what to do. There were some Muslims who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said if Muslims decided to leave Bosnia, is that what you meant, or --

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: If Muslims decided to break Yugoslavia up and to go their own separate way, away from Yugoslavia. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the essence of that plan, or the gist of the plan was about Yugoslavia, whether Yugoslavia would remain a state or whether it would be broken up?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please define what the Serbian side wanted, or rather, what was the policy and desire of you SDS members?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: The objective of the SDS, its foundation and its struggle was to fight for Yugoslavia, for Yugoslavia to stay as it was, because that was the only way we knew how to live. It was the only acceptable solution for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you also mentioned the SDA Crisis Staff, do you know anything about the arming of the Muslims in the Zvornik municipality at the end of 1991 and in 1992 prior to the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Since we knew that they had established the Patriotic League and that in the village of Godus they took up positions, there's still a memorial plaque there in that village testifying to that. When they did that, we went to Belgrade taking along the relevant documentation with a request that we too be armed in view of the negative experience we had from World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you repeat what the name of the village was, the one you referred to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: The village is called Godus and it's in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, you mentioned the ministry in Belgrade, can you tell us specifically what ministry this was, if it was a ministry at all?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: No. I misspoke. It was the Municipal Board for the Serbs living outside Serbia. There was never a ministry with that title as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you repeat the name of the body?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Board for the care of the Serbs outside Serbia, and I know that -- and it was a body attached to the Assembly of the Serbs, and I know that we were in the Assembly building, that's where we were housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell us who was the head of the board, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: At the time we left there, it was Radmilo Bogdanovic. At the time we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who went to visit the Assembly board for the Serbs outside Serbia together with you?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: From what I recall, there was Branko Grujic, Jovo Mijatovic, and I'm not sure if there was anyone else with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you took along some sort of documentation. What documentation was it and who did you present it to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: It was a video-clip. When I talked about the contacts we had with the people in the office next door, well, one of those people gave us footage featuring the Patriotic League and people lined up with automatic weapons. There was around 100 people lined up and they were fully equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You tell us that Bogdanovic was there, do you know what role he played before he took up the position with the Assembly board?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, I know from the mass media, that he was minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of which country?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Serbia, or rather, he was the Republic of Serbia minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you visited the Assembly board, who did Radmilo Bogdanovic refer you to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: He referred me to Radoslav Kostic, to Darda.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did Radmilo Bogdanovic tell you about weapons? Were you to expect any sort of assistance and from whom?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: He recommended that I should tell the story to Kostic, that there was a Trusine place in Croatia, that they had weapons available from the TO and that we should try and obtain some weapons from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Kostic refer you to the JNA which was present at the time? I am sorry, Bogdanovic, did he refer you to the JNA as a potential sponsor?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Since it was common knowledge that Slovenians, Croats and Muslims did not want to responds to call-ups for the JNA, one of the instructions was that we should liaise as far as possible with the JNA, that we should pull our ranks together and obtain weapons from them because there was already a disproportion between the assets that they had and the men at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the JNA was in need of men and you were in need of weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What view did the SDS take with regard to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: It was amicable and we were told that we should be forthcoming to any and all requests we received from the JNA, because the JNA was working toward keeping Yugoslavia together and this was something that they advocated through the mass media until the very last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs from the Zvornik municipality, did they respond to the JNA call-ups in late 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, in as many numbers as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which units were manned by people from the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: For the most part, they were units which withdrew from Slovenia and in part from Croatia. I know that there was a large strength unit in Zvornik which had been pulled out from Jastrebarsko in Croatia, so they were for the most part units that had been withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The unit which had been pulled out of Jastrebarsko, was it a tank brigade which was deployed to the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, it was a tank brigade under the command of Colonel Tacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and I am referring to March and April of 1992, where were Tacic's units billeted, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I know that most of the tanks were parked in Karakaj at Celopek next to the community centre there. They had units in Mali Zvornik, they had some units at Caparde, in Sekovici, at Branjevo and Pilica in the direction of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I know the geography of the area well, these were strategic locations around Zvornik and parts of the Republic of Serbia that these tank units were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, as well as in other locations that were strategically important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I heard you say in Serbian -- but I'll ask you again. Where else were Tacic's units deployed?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: At bridges. I mentioned Celopek, Pilica, Branjevo, Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in the town of Zvornik, were there or are there bridges between Zvornik and Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: There is a bridge which separates Zvornik from Serbia and it's no more than 150 metres, the distance that it spans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how many other locations in Zvornik have bridges, dams and such-like features?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: The municipality of Zvornik has three bridges for road traffic, a railway traffic bridge, and a hydroelectric plant which was also of service to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And all these features, were manned by JNA units?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, who is Dusko Vujkovic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I think there's another typo there, I think I spoke of Dusko Vukotic who is a reserve officer -- no, he is an officer who hails from Zvornik but was in service somewhere in Serbia. Then at the start of the war he came to Zvornik where he spent his entire time as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that he was an active-duty officer and that he came to Zvornik. Do you know anything of this individual's role in the arming of the Serbian population in the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes, this was yet another way of arming people because he had a position with the JNA as an officer, he could obtain weapons and that was the sort of assistance he provided for the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Vaso Eric, who is he?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Vaso Eric was a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS and the president of the Zvornik court. I probably mentioned him as part of the arming effort because he was good friends with Colonel Milosevic who was commander of the Romanija Corps or the Romanija Brigade, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question, Mr. Petrovic. You earlier said that that is another typo when Mr. Petrovic asked you about Dusko Vukovic, where did you find that typo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was just one letter that was different. It's not Vukovic but rather Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said that another typo. I observed you when you said it, I don't think you were looking to your screen. Did you want to refer to your statement where it is also said Dusko Vukovic, were you referring to that or were you referring to your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the statement here. Vukovic is written here and it's in the context of the arming and I know it's Vukotic, but we have another person Vuckovic, that's different story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just, when you said that is another typo, I wondered whether you referred to your statement as we find it on paper, is that what you refer to or did you refer to anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I noticed the typo when I was reviewing it, but I just didn't think it so important. His name is Vukotic and he lives in Zvornik today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic. Well, at the same time, I would like you to finish in one or two minutes so that we can instruct the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last question had to do with Vaso Eric and his role. You said that Vaso Eric was the president of the court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many pieces of weaponry were obtained through him?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but perhaps most of the weapons came through him since he had good connections, the man was the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Brigade and I think that it was through that channel that most of the weapons were obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he, as the president of the court, was supposed to prosecute people who had unlawful weapons, at any rate, he was supposed to be involved in trying persons in possession unlawfully of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, the justice administration broke down completely. I did not dare to go into a Muslim village as a Serb, as my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the judiciary was practically non-operational in March, April, May, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-026
utterances.text: Well, even before that. As of November or December 1991, no authority was operational. It was the law of the highwayman and those who were strong could wield power.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I will stop here and resume my examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Witness JF-026, we'll soon adjourn for the day. Some material has been prepared, that is material from the -- your testimony in the first case. Would you please be so kind to review that material this evening and tomorrow morning so as to tell us or give answers to questions similar to the one that is were put to you today, that is to review it and to point at specific places where you would say that the content of your testimony is not correct. I do understand that you have already worked on the -- your testimony in the second case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it would be appreciated if you write down the pages on which you find any inaccuracies and then to explain to us tomorrow where they are and what they are. This might take some time. Are you willing to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it in writing, Judge. I only have the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you'll get it. It has been prepared and you'll be provided with it. Madam Registrar will take care of that. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might suggest an instruction, the the version that he has -- that he'll have in his own language does not have the same pagination as our English. I was going to suggest that he be instructed to draw a line under any sentence which he believes to be either untrue or inaccurate and then in the margin to write what would be the correct statement that he wishes to make and perhaps that might be an orderly way for us to be able to go through it and to keep track of where we are in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do that, underline the phrases which you consider to be not correct. Not to say that you could say more about these matters, but just where you think that the testimony is not correct. I further would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way whether that communication is about your testimony already given today or still to be given in the days to come. And I finally would like to instruct you not to seek eye contact in this court with any of the accused in order to have unspoken communication between you and the accused. Would you please keep that in mind for the days to come as well. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 2nd of December, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
